To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the reputation hybrids are the best for fairness, the reciprocity/reputational hybrid is the best for efficiency and fairness when free-riding is present, and the reciprocity hybrids are best when free-riding is absent.

1) the three basic incentive mechanisms lie along a trade-off between efficiency and fairness; 2) all three hybrids are efficient and fairer than the basic algorithms; 3) reputation-based hybrids can match the bootstrapping speed of altruism, but only the hybrid that includes reciprocity can prevent free-riding; 4) the performance of the three hybrids are similar, but the reciprocity/reputaion hybrid is better when free-riding is present; 5)

(i) the three hybrid incentive mechanisms all have similar efficiency and fairness, and that (ii) the reciprocity/reputations hybrid has the best performance in the presence of free-riders, while altruism has the worst.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the performance analysis of incentive mechanisms for cooperative computing in peer-to-peer settings.
the design, analysis, and implementation of incentive mechanisms for cooperative computing in the Internet of Everything.
the problem of designing incentive mechanisms that encourage users to upload information to the Internet.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the reciprocity/reputations hybrid is a better incentive mechanism for cooperative computing than the other three hybrids, and that the reciprocity hybrid is better than the other two.
the hybrid reciprocity/reputation algorithm is the best choice for an incentive mechanism.
reciprocity-based algorithms are the best for scenarios in which free-riders need to be discouraged, whereas reputation-based algorithms are the better choice in cases where free-riders do not exist.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we provide a theoretical foundation for the design of incentive mechanisms for cooperative computing, and we show that the reputation/reciprocity hybrid is the most effective incentive mechanism in the context of cooperative computing.

we have developed a novel framework for analyzing incentive mechanisms, and we have shown that the reputation-based hybrid is the most fair incentive mechanism, while the reciprocity-based hybrid is the best when free-riding is a problem.
the performance of incentive mechanism is highly dependent on the design of the algorithm.
The main takeaway from our work is that
reputation-based algorithms, which have been used extensively in peer-to-peer systems, are not optimal for cooperative computing systems.

the choice of incentive mechanism is a crucial design decision that should be made with the tradeoff between fairness (i.e., bootstrapping new users) and efficiency (i.e., preventing free-riding) in mind.
the design of an incentive mechanism should depend on the application scenario, and that a hybrid design may yield better performance than a single component.
